articles.title: 'Had enough': Thousands protest in Prague against Czech government's public media funding overhaul
articles.summary: Thousands of people gathered in Czech Republic capital Prague on Sunday to protest against thec government's plans to overhaul the funding of public
articles.body: Thousands of people gathered in Czech Republic capital Prague on Sunday to protest against thec government's plans to overhaul the funding of public television and radio, warning that the changes could undermine media independence and expose broadcasters to political pressure.The demonstration in the historic Old Town Square and surrounding streets followed an overnight vote in the lower house of parliament that advanced legislation to abolish licence fees paid by households and businesses and replace them with direct funding from the state budget.The bill, backed by Prime Minister Andrej Babis's governing coalition, received initial approval in the early hours of Saturday after lawmakers moved it unexpectedly onto the agenda and curtailed debate. The legislation is now at the committee stage and must clear further parliamentary votes, including approval by the upper house, before becoming law.Why are Czechs protesting?The proposed reform would cut funding for Czech Television and Czech Radio by around 15 per cent, potentially from next year. Critics argue that replacing licence fees with allocations from the state budget would make public broadcasters more vulnerable to political interference.Protesters accused the government of pushing through the changes without adequate public scrutiny. Demonstrators chanted slogans including “We've had enough” and “Resignation”, demanding that the draft be withdrawn and that the government allow a thorough public debate.Meanwhile, Babis has rejected suggestions that the plan threatens media independence, saying it is intended to improve transparency in funding.The proposal has drawn criticism from opposition parties and international media organisations, which have called for greater scrutiny of the legislation. Some opponents have compared the plans with changes introduced in Hungary under former prime minister Viktor Orban, whose government oversaw an expansion of pro-government media, and reforms in Slovakia under Prime Minister Robert Fico.The European Broadcasting Union, Reporters Without Borders, the International Press Institute and the European Federation of Journalists are among the organisations that have raised concerns. The European Broadcasting Union and 15 other groups also called for further debate and warned against measures that could threaten the broadcasters' financial sustainability.Czech President Petr Pavel has called for greater expert scrutiny, saying the country was among the few in central and eastern Europe where public-service and private media systems worked well.On the other hand, Mikulas Minar, a leading organiser from the Million Moments for Democracy group, told the crowd, “You've gone too far, we won't let this country be destroyed.” He also criticised the timing of the parliamentary vote, saying, “It is mafia syndicates or the Soviet Politburo who make decisions at 4:36.”For some protesters, the proposed changes evoked memories of the country's history of state control over broadcasting.Milan Kotal, a 94-year-old demonstrator, said: “In my lifetime there have already been two state takeovers of our television in Prague: once by the Nazis during the war and then by the Communists until 1989.”“Today the government is allowing itself things we cannot accept,” he added.Public media employees have announced plans to go on strike on November 3, while organisers have called a larger rally at Prague's Letna Park on November 15, two days before the anniversary of the 1989 Velvet Revolution that ended communist rule in Czechoslovakia.Public broadcasters remain an important source of news in the country. Czech Television is the country's most-watched broadcaster across major age groups, while public media rank among the most trusted news sources, according to a 2025 Reuters Institute survey.You use AI every day. articles.summary: JHANSI: Muskan walks into a hotel room with her husband and another employee.
articles.body: JHANSI: Muskan walks into a hotel room with her husband and another employee. Within 5 seconds, she suddenly collapses backwards near the doorway, her head hitting the ground. Her husband immediately picks her up and carries her inside.The sequence captured on CCTV has raised questions about what happened in the moments before 28-year-old Muskan Simolia collapsed. She died the following morning, and her father has accused her husband of murder.Muskan, who married a bank manager nearly four months ago, was staying with her husband, Nilesh, a resident of Vidisha in Madhya Pradesh, at a hotel in Jhansi’s Sipri Bazaar police station area. According to police, the couple checked into the hotel on Friday night. The following morning, Muskan was taken to the district hospital, where doctors declared her dead.The circumstances surrounding her sudden collapse are now under investigation. Police have detained Nilesh for questioning, while the postmortem examination is expected to help establish the cause of death.CCTV captures moments before woman’s collapseThe CCTV footage reportedly shows Muskan entering the hotel room with Nilesh and another employee. Shortly afterwards, she suddenly falls backwards near the doorway. Nilesh is then seen lifting her and carrying her inside the room.SP City Preeti Singh said police inspected the hotel and examined the CCTV footage, which showed Muskan suddenly collapsing outside the room.According to Nilesh, Muskan fell while the couple were preparing to check out of the hotel. Hotel staff subsequently helped take her to the hospital.However, the circumstances that led to her collapse remain unclear. The footage captures the fall but does not, by itself, establish what caused it or whether any assault took place.Muskan’s father, Ramji Lal Ahirwar, has questioned the circumstances surrounding her death, pointing to injuries on her head and alleging that she was assaulted. He has demanded a thorough investigation into the incident.Father alleges husband had concealed first marriageMuskan married Nilesh on June 29 this year, according to her father. Ahirwar alleged that the family later learnt that Nilesh was already married and that his first wife lived in Indore.The revelation reportedly led to frequent quarrels between the couple. Her father has cited the alleged marital discord while raising suspicions about the circumstances surrounding his daughter’s death.Ahirwar has accused Nilesh of murdering Muskan. Police have detained him for questioning, but the allegation has not been established, and investigators are yet to determine the cause of death.Woman had returned home to prepare for railway examMuskan had returned to her parental home in Jhansi on October 10 to prepare for a railway junior engineer examination scheduled for October 28, her father said.Ahirwar alleged that Nilesh arrived in Jhansi on October 23 and took Muskan with him on the pretext of visiting his aunt. He claimed that Nilesh instead took her to a hotel.The couple checked into the hotel on Friday night. The following morning, Muskan collapsed near the room’s entrance and was subsequently taken to the district hospital, where she was declared dead.Her father has questioned the sequence of events and demanded that investigators establish what happened before she collapsed and whether the injuries on her head were linked to her death.Postmortem report awaitedPolice have sent Muskan’s body for postmortem examination. articles.title: Google CEO Sundar Pichai admits that cloud business is forgoing short-term revenues to make up for ...
articles.summary: Google is giving its AI researchers priority over cloud customers.
articles.body: Google is giving its AI researchers priority over cloud customers. CEO Sundar Pichai has confirmed that the company is forgoing short-term Google Cloud revenue by directing some of its limited computing capacity toward developing advanced AI models. The decision comes as demand for Google’s cloud services continues to rise and some customers struggle to secure additional capacity.​“Our cloud business is at any given moment in time forgoing short-term revenues because we are making compute trade-offs to support frontier AI development,” Pichai told Alex Kantrowitz during an interview on the Big Technology Podcast​Frontier AI refers to the development of models that aim to reach the highest level of current capabilities. These systems require massive computing power to train and run, creating competition between Google’s internal research and paying cloud customers.​Google Cloud generated $24.8 billion in second-quarter revenue, up 82% from a year earlier, while its contracted backlog reached about $514 billion. However, Pichai said the company must maintain enough computing power for Google DeepMind’s research, and its other businesses must plan around that need.​Why Google is prioritising AI research​Pichai described access to computing power for Google DeepMind as “non-negotiable.” He argued that developing advanced models gives Google an early view of new AI abilities and helps the company prepare products for future uses.​He also expects frontier models to help researchers build their successors through recursive self-improvement. This means an AI system assists with the research, coding, or testing required to create a more capable model.​Pichai rejected suggestions that Google should focus only on smaller, less expensive models such as Gemini Flash.​“We won’t do it any other way,” he said about competing at the AI frontier. “We’ve been thinking about the AI frontier for well over a decade now.”​Google Cloud customers face limited computing capacity​Google’s decision comes amid a shortage of the chips, servers, and data-center space needed to run AI services. Pichai said accommodating a new customer seeking computing capacity in 2027 would be “incredibly difficult to do.”​“Everyone wishes you had 2x of what you had planned for,” he said, describing the shortage across the technology industry.​Building additional capacity requires decisions years before customers can use it. “The compute we have today is a function of decisions I made in 2024,” Pichai said.​Alphabet expects to spend $195 billion to $205 billion on capital projects in 2026, with much of that investment supporting AI and cloud infrastructure.​Its regulatory filing showed that Google Cloud had $513.9 billion in contracted revenue waiting to be recognised at the end of June. Alphabet’s second-quarter filing said slightly more than half of that backlog is expected to become revenue within two years.​Demand is also coming from Google’s own products. Pichai said Gemini 4 Argon processed almost 25 trillion tokens in its first 72 hours, about three times what Gemini 3 handled over the same period. He added that Google was already capacity-constrained while serving the model.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.body: VIJAYAWADA: The India Meteorological Department (IMD) has issued a yellow warning for Srikakulam and Vizianagaram districts on Monday, forecasting heavy rainfall at isolated places as Cyclone Arnab approaches the Andhra Pradesh coast.The weather agency has also issued red and orange alerts for several districts for Tuesday (October 27) and Wednesday (October 28), warning of extremely heavy to very heavy rainfall that could disrupt normal life.The system was centred over the east-central and adjoining west-central Bay of Bengal, about 590 km northwest of Sri Vijaya Puram in the Andaman Islands, 650 km east-southeast of Visakhapatnam, 730 km east-southeast of Kakinada, 830 km east of Machilipatnam and 910 km east of Bapatla in Andhra Pradesh.It is very likely to move west-northwestwards and intensify further into a severe cyclonic storm over the west-central Bay of Bengal by Monday midnight, and into a very severe cyclonic storm over the same region on Tuesday (October 27).Thereafter, it is very likely to move northwestwards and cross the coasts of Andhra Pradesh and Yanam between Bapatla and Visakhapatnam as a very severe cyclonic storm, with maximum sustained wind speeds of 115–125 kmph and gusts of up to 140 kmph, by the forenoon of October 28.The India Meteorological Department (IMD) has issued a red alert, warning of extremely heavy rainfall, for Tuesday (October 27) in Kakinada, Konaseema, East Godavari, West Godavari and Eluru districts, as well as Yanam in Puducherry. articles.body: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and IDF chief of staff general Eyal Zamir are reportedly at odds over a possible military operation. The reported disagreement comes just a day before Israel heads to polls, with speculation that the operation could involve a new strike on Iran.According to Israel's Channel 12, citing anonymous sources, Zamir sought further discussions and written legal authorisation from Netanyahu before proceeding with the operation. The report did not specify the nature of the proposed action.A military source told Channel 12, “This relates to an action that could lead to a flare-up with Iran, at a sensitive and dramatic moment, creating this potential miscalculation.” Other unnamed sources expressed concern that Israel's political leadership could be trying to use the Iran issue for political gain.However, Netanyahu dismissed the allegations as “nonsense” in an interview with Israel's Channel 14, according to the Times of Israel. In an earlier television appearance, he said he had instructed the IDF and Mossad to work towards toppling the Iranian regime.The reported disagreement comes amid heightened political tensions ahead of the election, with pollsters projecting a close contest between Netanyahu and his main rival, Gadi Eisenkot.The reported face-off comes as US President Donald Trump again endorsed Netanyahu on Sunday, reiterating his support for the Israeli prime minister and urging voters to back him in Tuesday's election."To the people of Israel, to those who haven’t seen it, I am attaching the Endorsement I gave one week ago to your Prime Minister, Bibi Netanyahu. As everyone is aware, including the enemy, Bibi and I have had a great relationship in winning together ... When you go to the Polls, please remember that Bibi has been an outstanding Warrior Prime Minister!”The US President further wrote on Truth Social, “Israel was called The Little Satan, with the United States being called The Big Satan, by some very evil people. There can no longer be the chant heard around the World of “Death to America, Death to Israel,” and there won’t be. Vote for Bibi Netanyahu for Prime Minister, we have to finish the job that we started."Israeli PM Netanyahu also posted an AI-generated image on social media on Sunday depicting a nuclear explosion in Tel Aviv. Two days before the election, he warned that voting for anyone other than him could expose Israelis to the danger of a “second Holocaust.”Quoting right-wing activist Yuval Blumberg's statements, Netanyahu's post read,"The State of Israel is in real and tangible existential danger. If the Iranians acquire nuclear weapons, nothing will ever be the same again. Everything is so trivial compared to the existential threat of Iran and the Shiite axis."The post further argued that the remaining period of Trump's presidency presented a window to address the Iranian threat, while questioning whether a future US administration would offer the same opportunity.The final projections for Tuesday's election, published on October 23, indicated continued political gridlock. Neither the ruling coalition nor the opposition bloc was projected to secure enough support to form a government following the vote.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Kochi Mercedes hit-and-run: Judge’s minor son drives car at high speed, kills man; released on bail, now taken into custody again after protests
articles.summary: KOCHI: Police took the 17-year-old son of an additional sessions judge into custody again after protests by the family of a man killed when Mercedes-Benz
articles.body: KOCHI: Police took the 17-year-old son of an additional sessions judge into custody again after protests by the family of a man killed when Mercedes-Benz allegedly driven by the minor rammed into his scooter in Cheranelloor, Kochi, in the early hours of Sunday.Police had initially registered a case of causing death by negligence and released the boy on bail from the police station.However, following protests by the victim’s family and a preliminary investigation indicating that the car was being driven at high speed, police invoked Section 105 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), which deals with culpable homicide not amounting to murder.The deceased, Jayabalakrishnan, 55, a resident of South Chittoor, ran a roadside eatery. He was returning home on his scooter after closing his shop when the accident occurred around 2.20am on Container Road near Marapparambu in Cheranelloor.Both vehicles were travelling towards Kalamassery, and a preliminary investigation indicated that the Mercedes hit the scooter from behind. The car is registered in the judge’s name.The initial release of the minor triggered protests outside Cheranelloor police station, where Jayabalakrishnan’s son and daughter, accompanied by activists, demanded that the accused be taken into custody and produced before the Juvenile Justice Board.As the agitation intensified and more people gathered in support of the family, senior police officers intervened. Police subsequently reached the judge’s residence, took the boy into custody and produced him before the board late at night.During the protest, Jayabalakrishnan’s daughter fainted and was taken to hospital, police said.The victim’s family also demanded that a case be registered against the judge for allegedly allowing his minor son to drive the car. Police said they had sought legal opinion on whether the judge could be arraigned in the case and would take a decision on Monday.An earlier police statement said the minor had undergone a medical examination, with preliminary findings indicating that he had not consumed alcohol. A detailed report was awaited.Police sources said the boy had claimed that the scooter suddenly swerved to avoid waterlogging and that he could not stop the car in time to prevent the collision. Heavy rain had lashed the area during the early hours of Sunday.Jayalakshmi, a relative of the victim, described the accident scene as horrifying, pointing to the damage to the vehicles and the distance at which the victim’s footwear and helmet were found.She also alleged that the judge had spoken disrespectfully to the family when they questioned why his minor son had been allowed to drive. The family said it would pursue the case.The incident comes less than three weeks after another fatal crash in Kochi on October 11, when a Mini Cooper allegedly driven at high speed by a 19-year-old who had consumed alcohol hit a scooter, killing three youths. The accused remains in judicial custody.Meanwhile, Youth Congress leader Shajahan P Y had approached state home minister Ramesh Chennithala, seeking action under Section 199A of the Motor Vehicles Act, which provides for action against the guardian or vehicle owner when a juvenile commits a traffic offence using a vehicle.The law provides for exceptions if the guardian or owner can establish that the offence occurred without their knowledge or that they exercised due diligence to prevent it.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Kochi | Silver Rate in Kochi | Bank Holidays in Kochi | Public Holidays in KochiStay updated with the latest Kochi news. articles.title: Five economic challenges ahead as Brazil’s Lula da Silva wins fourth term, defeats Flávio Bolsonaro
articles.summary: Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva faces mounting public debt, persistently high interest rates, rising household indebtedness and political
articles.body: Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva faces mounting public debt, persistently high interest rates, rising household indebtedness and political hurdles to economic reforms as he prepares to begin his fourth term in January, despite the economy performing better than expected in recent years.Lula’s victory over conservative challenger Flávio Bolsonaro in Sunday’s presidential runoff has secured another term for the left-wing leader. However, growing fiscal pressures and a conservative-led Congress could complicate efforts to implement his economic agenda.According to a Reuters report by Marcela Ayres and Bernardo Caram, Lula will have to navigate five major economic challenges, ranging from controlling government borrowing and inflation to implementing a sweeping tax overhaul.1. Rising public debt and fiscal pressureBrazil’s public debt has increased by more than 10 percentage points during Lula’s current term, surpassing 82% of gross domestic product (GDP) and pushing up borrowing costs.Years of rising mandatory expenditure have left the federal government with limited flexibility in its budget, with less than 8% of spending available for adjustments.Lula has sent mixed signals on fiscal discipline, at times dismissing concerns about public debt as “nonsense” while arguing that stronger economic growth would help address the problem.His administration has pledged to retain the existing fiscal framework, which limits spending growth and establishes targets for the primary balance, or government revenue minus expenditure excluding interest payments on public debt. Officials have also indicated that the rules could be tightened.However, meeting these targets could prove difficult as Lula has promised to increase the minimum wage faster than inflation. Such increases also raise pension expenditure, adding to the cost of welfare benefits that his government has already expanded.2. High interest rates and persistent inflationBrazil continues to face elevated borrowing costs and inflationary pressures despite signs of an economic slowdown.Interest rates stand at 13.75%, while annual inflation is 4.6%, above the central bank’s tolerance range of 1.5% to 4.5%. The central bank delivered its fifth consecutive rate cut last month as economic activity showed signs of weakening.However, financial markets expect inflation to remain above the official 3% target until as late as 2029.Lula has pledged to bring interest rates down through greater fiscal discipline while protecting social programmes. Economists, however, argue that faster rate reductions would require cuts in government spending.Balancing lower borrowing costs with continued social expenditure will therefore be a key challenge for the incoming administration.3. Mounting debt among households and businessesHigh interest rates have also increased the financial burden on Brazilian households and businesses, with a record number of borrowers falling behind on repayments.According to credit bureau Serasa, nearly 84 million Brazilians and 9.3 million businesses are behind on debt payments.The growing debt burden has fuelled public dissatisfaction despite favourable economic indicators, including record-low unemployment and wage growth outpacing inflation.Lula plans to introduce another round of debt relief, including discounted purchases of distressed household loans from banks and tax debt forgiveness for some small business owners.However, analysts have cautioned that such measures may provide only temporary relief without addressing the underlying causes of indebtedness.The government has also discussed with the central bank ways to curb excessive reliance on easily available but expensive credit, including credit cards and unsecured consumer loans. No detailed proposals have been announced so far.4. Conservative Congress could obstruct reformsLula is likely to face difficulties securing congressional support for his economic agenda after voters elected the most conservative legislature since Brazil returned to democracy in the 1980s.Although Lula defeated Flávio Bolsonaro in the presidential runoff, Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party and its allies are expected to control both chambers of Congress.The political balance could complicate efforts to reduce tax breaks and introduce other fiscal measures. Lula’s aides have indicated that the government will continue seeking to curtail tax exemptions, but lawmakers have repeatedly resisted proposals that increase the effective tax burden.During his current term, Lula has also struggled to secure Senate approval for nominees to key institutions, including the Supreme Court, central bank, securities regulator and antitrust watchdog.The rightward shift in Congress could make such appointments and other legislative priorities more difficult to advance during his fourth term.5. Uncertainty over sweeping tax reformsLula secured congressional approval in 2023 for a major overhaul of Brazil’s consumption tax system, with a new value-added tax scheduled to take effect in January.However, with fewer than three months remaining before implementation, the government has yet to disclose the effective tax rate. Independent analysts estimate that it could be around 28%.The administration has also delayed submitting legislation to regulate a new tax on products considered harmful to public health or the environment, including cigarettes and alcohol.The delay, partly driven by concerns about a public backlash during the election campaign, could postpone revenue collection from the proposed levy and has drawn criticism over the government’s handling of tax policy.Implementing the consumption tax overhaul while resolving outstanding questions over rates and additional levies will be another major test for Lula’s administration as it seeks to balance revenue generation, economic growth and household affordability.You use AI every day. articles.title: Can an unmarried daughter claim maintenance from her father? Bombay high court answers
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Bombay high court has upheld a family court order directing a father to pay maintenance of Rs 7,000 each to his unmarried daughter and son,
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Bombay high court has upheld a family court order directing a father to pay maintenance of Rs 7,000 each to his unmarried daughter and son, ruling that the daughter could continue to receive maintenance even after attaining the majority. The court also said the father could seek a change in the maintenance payable to his son before the appropriate forum.In its October 13, 2026, order, the Nagpur bench of the high court dismissed the father's challenge to the family court, Nagpur's December 7, 2019, order.Why did the father challenge the maintenance order?According to the court order, the family court had directed the father, a teacher earning Rs 71,000 a month, to pay Rs 7,000 each to his two children. It denied maintenance to his wife, who was also a teacher and earned Rs 40,000 a month.The father argued that both the children had attained majority and were no longer entitled to maintenance under Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC). He then argued that he had to maintain his elderly parents also.He further contended that his unmarried daughter, who was 23 when he filed the revision petition, should seek maintenance under Section 20(3) of the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956 (HAMA), rather than under Section 125 of the CrPC.The father also challenged maintenance for his son, who attained majority while the revision petition was pending.The wife and children opposed the petition, arguing that the daughter should not be forced to start fresh proceedings after years of litigation. They also submitted that the son was a minor when the family court passed its order and remained unable to maintain himself.Why did the high court uphold maintenance for the children?Justice Mehroz K Pathan noted that the son was a minor when the family court passed its order in 2019. His subsequent attainment of majority did not make the original order incorrect.On the daughter's claim, the court held that the availability of another legal remedy under the HAMA did not automatically prevent her from claiming maintenance under Section 125 of the CrPC, particularly when the father had failed to show that she could maintain herself.The court relied on the Supreme Court's judgment in Jagdish Jugtawat v Manju Lata, which upheld maintenance for an unmarried daughter after she attained majority. The Supreme Court had observed:“The right of a minor girl for maintenance from parents after attaining majority till her marriage is recognized in Section 20(3) of the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act,” the court noted.The high court said that the family court had committed no error in granting maintenance to the unmarried daughter, taking into account the legal position recognised by the Supreme Court.“In so far as the grievance of the applicant that the non-applicant no.3 has attained majority during the pendency of the present application can be very well raised in an application under Section 127 of Cr.P.C. to be filed before the appropriate forum,” the court added.Section 127 of the CrPC provides for altering a maintenance order when circumstances change. The court thus left it open to the father to raise the issue before the appropriate forum.The high court also referred to a Delhi high court ruling concerning an adult son who was still studying and unable to support himself.“It cannot be said that the obligation of a father would come to an end and when his son reaches 18 years of age and the entire burden of his education and other expenses would fall only on the mother……,” the high court further added.The court then held that the family court's direction to pay Rs 7,000 each to the two children was not erroneous. It dismissed the father's revision petition, leaving the maintenance order undisturbed.

articles.title: In 1979, ABBA gave UNICEF the royalties from Chiquitita; 45 years later, the song had raised more than $5 million to help protect vulnerable children from violence, abuse and exploitation worldwide
articles.summary: A song that became a global pop hit in 1979 has continued to fund child-protection work decades after its release.
articles.body: A song that became a global pop hit in 1979 has continued to fund child-protection work decades after its release. Swedish pop group ABBA's Chiquitita had generated more than US$5 million for UNICEF by April 2024, helping support programmes that protect vulnerable children from violence, abuse and exploitation, according to the United Nations children's agency. The milestone marked 45 years since the band pledged the song's royalties to UNICEF.The song's enduring contribution comes from royalties generated whenever listeners purchase or stream it on platforms including Spotify, Apple Music and YouTube. Rather than being a one-time charitable donation, the arrangement has allowed the track to generate funding over several decades, supporting UNICEF's work to protect and rehabilitate children affected by violence.How ABBA's 1979 pledge beganThe story began on January 9, 1979, when ABBA performed at The Music for UNICEF Concert: A Gift of Song, held at the United Nations General Assembly in New York. The event brought together prominent musicians, including the Bee Gees, Donna Summer, Rod Stewart, John Denver and Earth, Wind & Fire, to raise awareness and funds for children's rights. According to UNICEF's historical account, participating artists gave the organisation rights to songs performed at the concert. The event was organised to mark the International Year of the Child, a United Nations initiative intended to draw attention to children's welfare and rights worldwide.ABBA pledged the future revenues from Chiquitita, a song written by Benny Andersson and Björn Ulvaeus and featuring Agnetha Fältskog on lead vocals. The song was subsequently released as a single in January 1979 and became one of the group's best-known recordings.The title is a Spanish term of endearment meaning “little girl” or “little one”. Over time, the song's association with UNICEF gave it a charitable legacy that extended beyond its popularity as a recording.From royalties to child-protection servicesThe money raised through Chiquitita has helped UNICEF support programmes aimed at preventing abuse and assisting children who have experienced violence. In 2014, ABBA decided to direct all proceeds from the song towards UNICEF's work protecting girls' rights in Guatemala. The funding has supported child psychology and protection services, including work in the country's Verapaz region, home to Indigenous Mayan communities. UNICEF says the royalties help pay the salaries and training costs of psychologists and social workers who provide support to survivors and work to prevent sexual abuse.A report published by UNICEF Guatemala on April 2, 2024, described how these services reach children in remote communities, where accessing specialist support can be difficult. Psychologists and social workers conduct home visits, provide therapy and coordinate with local services to help children receive appropriate care.The report identified a team of 19 psychologists and 11 social workers working in the departments of Alta Verapaz and Baja Verapaz. Many serve communities where language barriers, poverty and limited access to services can make it harder for children to seek assistance. The work also extends beyond individual therapy. UNICEF has supported hospital facilities for sexual-abuse screenings and referrals, while community outreach and local radio broadcasts help spread prevention messages in Q'eqchi', a language spoken by many Indigenous people in the region.Thousands reached through the programmeThe funding has supported measurable results. In 2023 alone, UNICEF reported that the royalties from Chiquitita helped provide assistance to 1,000 survivors of abuse in remote areas of Guatemala. More than 10,000 people received treatment or preventative support during the same year. These figures illustrate how revenue from a single recording can contribute to sustained services for vulnerable communities. The programme combines direct assistance for survivors with prevention efforts intended to address the circumstances that allow abuse to continue.UNICEF's report also highlights the work of local professionals who understand the communities they serve and speak their languages. Their familiarity with local conditions helps them build relationships with children and families, identify cases requiring intervention and connect survivors with appropriate services. The organisation has stressed that protecting children requires more than responding after abuse occurs. Investment in community services, prevention, training and local support systems is also necessary to create lasting change.A musical legacy that continuesABBA member Björn Ulvaeus reflected on the song's long-term impact in comments quoted in UNICEF Guatemala's 2024 report. Speaking in 2022, he said he had not expected the contribution to last so long or generate so much money, describing it as “the best legacy anyone could wish for”. The group expanded its support for UNICEF in 2021 by pledging royalties from its Christmas song Little Things for five years. That commitment supports UNICEF's wider child-protection work, particularly efforts to protect girls from violence and advance gender equality.The two songs demonstrate how music can provide an ongoing source of charitable funding. While Chiquitita continues to generate royalties through purchases and streaming, its significance now extends beyond the charts to the children and families receiving support through UNICEF programmes.Forty-five years after the original pledge, the song's contribution offers an example of how a decision made at a benefit concert can have a lasting impact. Its more than US$5 million in reported royalties represents not simply a fundraising milestone, but continued support for efforts to help children live free from violence, abuse and exploitation.You use AI every day. articles.title: After two decades, Jamia Millia Islamia orders student union polls within 15 days of constitution approval; students reject move, vow to continue stir
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Jamia Millia Islamia has ordered the resumption of students’ union elections, stating that polls will be held within 15 days of approval of the
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Jamia Millia Islamia has ordered the resumption of students’ union elections, stating that polls will be held within 15 days of approval of the union’s constitution.The university has also revoked suspension orders and show-cause notices issued to students during the ongoing protest and announced an inquiry into the conduct of security personnel during the agitation.However, protesting students have rejected the administration’s order, calling it ambiguous and insisting that the agitation will continue until their demands are addressed through clear, written commitments.An order issued by Registrar Md Mahtab Alam Rizvi on Monday, October 26, states that elections to the Jamia Millia Islamia Students’ Union (JMISU) will be held 15 days after the union’s constitution is approved. It also provides for a committee to inquire into the actions of security staff during the protest.The order came after the administration held talks with students who had submitted a list of demands, including the restoration of the elected students’ union, withdrawal of disciplinary action and an inquiry into alleged excesses by security personnel.According to the order, the protesting students have agreed to issue a public apology through a press conference for allegedly defamatory statements, actions or social media posts targeting the university administration during the agitation. The posts are to be taken down from social media platforms with immediate effect.The order states that the protest will be called off immediately following its issuance.However, the Jammu & Kashmir Students Association said the order did not provide a definite timeline for approval of the union’s constitution or address the students’ demand for the resignation of the proctor.“Assurances without concrete decisions and a clear roadmap cannot be treated as fulfilment of our demands,” the student organisation said in a statement, adding that the agitation would continue until the administration provided written commitments addressing their concerns.According to the association, Registrar Rizvi arrived on campus around 4.30am on Monday for talks with the protesters. He shared the administration’s order and urged the students to end their agitation, saying their demands had been met.The protest has centred on the demand for the restoration of JMISU, whose elections have not been held since 2006. Four students had been on an indefinite hunger strike, while other protesters sought a time-bound election schedule, withdrawal of disciplinary action and an inquiry into the conduct of security personnel.Amid escalating tensions, the university had earlier shifted classes across courses to online mode and advised students against visiting the campus. It had also announced that gates and libraries would remain closed until further notice.The administration had said a seven-member committee of professors held multiple rounds of talks with the protesters. A committee to draft the JMISU constitution was notified on October 21.Students, however, had argued that setting up the drafting committee was insufficient without a definite election timeline and student representation in the process.The latest order addresses some of their demands, including the withdrawal of disciplinary action and an inquiry into the conduct of security personnel. However, the lack of a fixed deadline for approval of the constitution remains a key point of contention.(With agency inputs)You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news. articles.title: 'Canada took advantage of US, but we're getting close to a deal': Trump claims 'no rush' to resume talks
articles.summary: US president Donald Trump has accused Canada of taking advantage of the United States through trade imbalances over several years, while expressing
articles.body: US president Donald Trump has accused Canada of taking advantage of the United States through trade imbalances over several years, while expressing confidence that the two countries could eventually reach an agreement that benefits the American economy.Speaking to FOX 2’s Roop Raj ahead of a rally in Michigan, Trump claimed Canada had earned billions of dollars annually at the expense of the US. However, he said discussions between the neighbouring countries were moving towards a possible resolution, according to the news agency ANI.“Canada has been making $90B/year off us for years and years. They've taken advantage of our country, but we're getting close to a deal... I love Canada; I love everything about it - other than some of the leaders,” Trump said.The US President also stressed that he was seeking a lasting agreement rather than a temporary arrangement, arguing that the final deal should deliver long-term economic benefits for the country.“I want to make the right deal. I'm not a short-term person, I'm a long-term. When the deal is made, it'll be a great deal for America,” he added.Trump says he is in no hurry to resume trade talksEarlier this month, Trump said he was in no rush to restart trade negotiations with Canada, accusing Ottawa of treating Washington unfairly. He also insisted that Canada would have to act honestly for any future agreement to move forward.Asked whether negotiations would resume before the US midterm elections, Trump offered no timeline and questioned Canada's conduct in its trade relationship with the US.“I don't know. Canada behaves very badly with the United States and I don't know,” he said.Trump further alleged that Washington had discovered Canadian tariffs that he claimed had previously gone unnoticed by others. However, he did not specify which tariffs he was referring to.“We caught them in the act; they charged us a lot of tariffs that nobody knew about except me. And it will work out eventually, but I don't know about I'm in no rush,” he said.His remarks indicated that an early resumption of talks was not a priority, although he maintained that the dispute could eventually be resolved.Trump alleges imbalance in US-Canada tradeTrump reiterated his criticism of the commercial relationship between the two countries, claiming that Canada benefited disproportionately from its economic ties with the United States.“You know, Canada does all their business with us, we do very little business with them,” he said.He also argued that Canada needed to demonstrate greater transparency and fairness in its dealings with Washington.“And all we ask of one thing in Canada, they have to be honest. They are not honest with the United States; they've been ripping us off for years,” Trump added.Despite his criticism of Canadian leaders and trade practices, Trump expressed optimism that a future agreement could resolve the dispute. He did not provide further details about the proposed deal or indicate when negotiations might be concluded.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: “Next year, I will give one of my SpaceX shares to…”: Elon Musk’s proposed $10.6 billion giveaway could reach 72 million young people in America; but who will qualify
articles.summary: Elon Musk has announced plans to give every child in America a share of SpaceX in 2027, a proposal that could involve tens of millions of recipients and
articles.body: Elon Musk has announced plans to give every child in America a share of SpaceX in 2027, a proposal that could involve tens of millions of recipients and billions of dollars in stock. The pledge came hours after the billionaire criticised artificial intelligence company Anthropic for planning to place part of its equity in a public benefit fund, suggesting instead that shares should go directly to people. Musk has not explained who would qualify, how the transfers would work or whether the plan would use existing investment accounts for children. According to a Forbes report, based on current estimates, the proposed giveaway could involve around 72 million young people.Elon Musk plans to give every American child a SpaceX share in 2027In the X (formerly Twitter) post on October 19, Musk said he would give one of his SpaceX shares to every American child in 2027, describing the proposed distribution as the first of several such initiatives. He did not set out a timetable or explain whether the offer would cover all children living in the country or only those meeting particular eligibility requirements.Forbes reported, the US Census Bureau estimated that about 21.1% of the country's 341.8 million residents were children, equivalent to roughly 72.1 million people. That figure includes citizens and non-citizens, and Musk has not clarified whether his pledge would extend to both groups.There is also no published explanation of how the shares would reach their intended recipients. The announcement does not establish whether parents would need to register their children, whether the stock would be held in dedicated accounts or whether any restrictions would apply to the eventual sale of the shares.SpaceX shares could put Musk's proposed giveaway at $10.6 billionThe financial scale of the pledge depends on the number of children who qualify and the value of SpaceX stock when the transfers take place. Using the Census Bureau's estimate of approximately 72.1 million people under 18 and the reported premarket share price of $147.52 on October 19, the total value would come to around $10.6 billion if each child received one share at that price.That calculation is an estimate, not a confirmed valuation of the proposed giveaway. SpaceX shares can change in value, and the number of eligible recipients has not been established. The final cost would also depend on the arrangements used to distribute the stock.Musk's personal holdings appear large enough to accommodate a transfer of this size, based on figures disclosed earlier in the year. As reported by Forbes, an SEC filing, an August filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission reported that he held 6.42 billion SpaceX shares as of June 30. The figure included stock held through trusts for which he serves as trustee, restricted shares and shares issuable through options.A distribution of 72 million shares would represent slightly more than 1% of that reported total.Anthropic's public benefit fund preceded the announcementThe pledge followed a separate announcement by Anthropic, the company behind the Claude artificial intelligence chatbot. On October 18, the company said it would commit at least 5% of its shares to a newly established Anthropic Public Benefit Fund.The proposed fund is intended to support charitable organisations and could also make direct distributions to selected groups of people. Anthropic described it as a wholly owned limited liability company, setting out a structure through which the company could direct resources towards public benefit activities. Musk responded to the announcement on X, “I recommend giving the shares directly to the public.”Elon Musk's SpaceX pledge raises questions over Trump AccountsThe US government's Trump Accounts programme could provide relevant context for Musk's proposal, although he has not said whether his plan is connected to it. Earlier in 2026, SpaceX president Gwynne Shotwell and her husband pledged to contribute one SpaceX share each to the accounts of more than two million American children under the programme. The initiative provides a framework for holding investments on behalf of young people.Elon Musk's SpaceX giveaway plan leaves transfer details unresolvedThe proposed distribution would come from a company in which Musk has a significant financial interest. Forbes estimated his net worth at $908.5 billion in its October 19 report, placing him at the top of its real-time billionaire rankings. His wealth is closely tied to his business holdings, including SpaceX and Tesla.The report also noted that SpaceX shares rose by more than 1% to $147.52 in premarket trading that Monday, alongside a broader recovery in US stock futures following the previous week's market losses. The quoted price provides a reference point for estimating the possible value of the giveaway, but it does not establish what the shares would be worth when they are distributed.You use AI every day. articles.title: In the late 1960s, artist John Craxton bought a chandelier from a London antiques shop for £250 after recognising Giacometti's work; decades later, it sold for £2.922 million at Christie's
articles.summary: A chandelier that an artist bought for £250 after spotting it in a London antiques shop sold for £2.922 million at Christie's in 2023, turning a chance
articles.body: A chandelier that an artist bought for £250 after spotting it in a London antiques shop sold for £2.922 million at Christie's in 2023, turning a chance discovery into one of the more remarkable stories of the art market. The bronze light fitting, created by Swiss sculptor Alberto Giacometti, had been recognised by British artist John Craxton in the late 1960s, when the shop had listed its maker as unknown. According to Christie's, Craxton paid all his savings for the piece and kept it for the rest of his life.The chandelier, titled Chandelier for Peter Watson, was sold at Christie's London auction on February 28, 2023. The final price of £2,922,000 included the buyer's premium, with the hammer price itself reaching £2.4 million. The result followed decades in which the object remained in Craxton's family home, largely away from public view. Christie's identifies the work as unique, conceived in 1946–47 and cast around 1947–49.A chance discovery in a London antiques shopCraxton, who lived from 1922 to 2009, encountered the chandelier at Elizabeth Denton's antiques shop in London's Marylebone area. Christie's recounts that he had visited intending to collect a bronze lion but struck his head on a low-hanging chandelier while leaving the shop. He immediately recognised the work as Giacometti's, despite the absence of an artist's attribution on its listing.The sculptor's identity was only part of the attraction. Craxton believed the chandelier had a connection to Peter Watson, an art collector and patron who had supported him earlier in his career. He paid £250 for it and subsequently displayed it in the music room of his family home in Hampstead, north London.The object remained there until Craxton's death in 2009. It also became part of the surroundings in which musicians and other cultural figures gathered for performances and recitals. Craxton's father, Harold, was a distinguished pianist, while his sister Janet was an accomplished oboist. The chandelier therefore spent decades in a setting connected to the family's musical life.Commissioned for a literary magazineThe chandelier's history began well before Craxton discovered it. Watson commissioned Giacometti to create it for the London offices of Horizon, a literary and cultural magazine he co-founded with critic Cyril Connolly in 1939. Watson, who lived from 1908 to 1956, was a wealthy patron of modern art. He collected works by European avant-garde artists and supported younger British painters, including Craxton and Lucian Freud. His backing helped artists pursue their work and brought modern European art into conversation with Britain's literary and cultural circles.According to Christie's, Watson visited Giacometti's Paris studio in 1946 or 1947 and commissioned the chandelier for Horizon's offices on Bedford Square in Bloomsbury. The magazine published writing by figures including W.H. Auden, George Orwell, E.M. Forster and Dylan Thomas.The chandelier occupied a central position in the offices, where its sculptural form made it more than a functional light fitting. When Horizon closed in 1950, the offices were cleared and the chandelier went into storage. Its subsequent journey to Denton's shop remains uncertain. Christie's says there is no surviving record explaining how it ended up there.Why Giacometti's design stands outGiacometti, who lived from 1901 to 1966, is widely known for his elongated bronze figures, but he also designed decorative objects, including lamps, vases and chandeliers. His work often blurred the boundary between sculpture and functional design. The chandelier is made of bronze with a golden-brown patina. It stands 134cm tall and measures 153.5cm across. Its branching arms extend from a central stem, with intricate detailing around the light fittings. A perforated sphere hangs beneath the central structure, creating a visual link with Giacometti's earlier Surrealist sculpture Boule suspendue (1930).Its design reflects the period when the artist was exploring both decorative objects and sculptural forms. The chandelier was also a rare commission: its connection to Watson and Horizon gave it a documented place in the cultural history of post-war London.From £250 to a multimillion-pound saleBefore the 2023 auction, the chandelier's authenticity had faced questions. The Craxton estate undertook a process to establish its provenance, and the work was examined by the Fondation Giacometti in Paris in December 2021. Its identity was subsequently confirmed, clearing the way for the Christie's sale. The auction attracted attention because the object's story combined an extraordinary price difference with a significant artistic and historical background. However, its importance extended beyond its market value.In July 2023, the UK government announced a temporary export deferral for the chandelier, valued at £2.922 million, to give a British institution an opportunity to acquire it. The Reviewing Committee on the Export of Works of Art and Objects of Cultural Interest said it met criteria relating to its connection with national history, aesthetic importance and significance for studying Giacometti's decorative work.The government highlighted the chandelier's role in the offices of Horizon, where art, literature and European cultural influences intersected in the years after the Second World War.You use AI every day. articles.title: Psychology says children who carry the same toy from room to room may be seeking more than entertainment
articles.summary: A toddler carrying a soft toy from the bedroom to the living room, insisting on taking it along during family outings or becoming upset when it is nowhere
articles.body: A toddler carrying a soft toy from the bedroom to the living room, insisting on taking it along during family outings or becoming upset when it is nowhere to be found may appear to be attached to a favourite plaything. But for some children, the object serves a purpose beyond entertainment: it offers familiarity, comfort and a sense of security as they navigate an unfamiliar or overwhelming world.Child-development researchers have studied this behaviour under the concept of transitional objects or attachment objects. These are familiar items, often soft toys, blankets or pieces of cloth, that children turn to for reassurance. Their significance lies not necessarily in what the object does, but in how the child feels when it is nearby.The American Academy of Pediatrics explains that such objects can help children cope with separation from caregivers, tiredness, distress and unfamiliar surroundings. Rather than being a sign of weakness or excessive dependence, attachment to a favourite object can be part of the normal process of growing towards independence.The comfort of something familiarYoung children experience many changes in a short period. They move between rooms, encounter unfamiliar people, begin attending preschool and gradually spend more time away from their primary caregivers. They are also learning to understand and communicate feelings they may not yet have the words to describe.A familiar toy can provide a sense of continuity through these transitions. Its texture, smell and appearance remain recognisable even when the surroundings change.In its guidance on transitional objects and security blankets, the American Academy of Pediatrics notes that children may develop a preference for such objects during infancy, often around eight to 12 months. The object can become particularly reassuring when a child is tired, upset or separated from a caregiver.This helps explain why a child might carry the same teddy bear through the house even when there are plenty of other toys available. The child may not be looking for a new activity at every stop. Simply having a familiar object close by may make the environment feel more manageable.Psychologist Donald Winnicott introduced the term transitional object in 1953 to describe the special relationship some young children develop with particular possessions. In this framework, the object helps bridge the child's experience of depending on a caregiver and gradually becoming more comfortable with independence.The concept does not mean that a toy replaces a parent or that every child needs one. Instead, it offers a way to understand why a seemingly ordinary possession can carry considerable emotional importance.What research says about carrying a favourite toyResearch suggests that attachment objects can play a role in how children cope with everyday stress, although the behaviour varies between children and families.A 2014 study published in Frontiers in Psychology examined attachment to inanimate objects and its relationship with early childcare. The researchers noted that children often turn to soft toys or blankets in vulnerable situations, such as when they are upset, ill, tired or in unfamiliar surroundings.The study also reviewed earlier experimental research in which children who had access to their preferred attachment objects in an unfamiliar play setting explored without showing distress for longer than children who lacked an attachment to the object. Their behaviour was comparable, in this respect, to that of children whose mothers were present.These findings offer a possible explanation for why some children want their favourite toy nearby even when a parent is in the next room. Familiarity with the object may help them feel secure enough to continue playing or exploring.However, the evidence should not be overstated. Carrying a toy from room to room has not, by itself, been established as a reliable measure of a child's emotional state. The research concerns attachment objects and responses to particular situations, not every instance of a child taking a toy along.A separate 1993 study published in Perceptual and Motor Skills observed 105 toddlers during daily separations from significant caregivers at childcare. The researchers found that attachment objects appeared to facilitate separation and reduce anxiety in mildly stressful situations.Taken together, these studies suggest that a familiar object may be one of the ways some young children manage transitions and cope with temporary separation.Why the same toy matters more than a new oneParents sometimes offer a replacement toy when a child's favourite becomes worn, dirty or damaged. Yet a new version may not provide the same reassurance, even if it looks almost identical.That preference may have something to do with the history the child associates with the original object.A 2016 study published in Cognitive Science examined young children's preference for unique, personally owned objects. In experiments involving 36 three-year-olds, researchers presented children with familiar objects they owned and comparable new alternatives.The children preferred their own objects in the relevant comparisons, suggesting that they placed special value on possessions connected to their personal history. Their preferences were not simply about which object looked newer or more attractive.The study was not specifically about toddlers carrying comfort toys between rooms, so it cannot explain every such behaviour. Nevertheless, it offers a useful insight: a possession can become meaningful because it is the child's own familiar object, not merely because of its appearance or function.Over time, a toy may become associated with bedtime routines, cuddles, family trips or moments when a child was comforted. A replacement cannot automatically reproduce those associations.For parents, this is a reason to avoid dismissing a favourite toy as interchangeable or assuming that buying a more attractive one will solve the problem.It may also be a way to manage big feelingsToddlers are still developing the ability to regulate emotions. They may become overwhelmed by frustration, fatigue, unfamiliar settings or changes in routine, and they cannot always explain what is bothering them.A favourite object can become part of the child's personal strategy for dealing with these feelings. Holding it, rubbing its fabric or simply keeping it within sight may be reassuring.A 2021 review in Current Opinion in Psychology examined the origins and development of attachment to objects. It describes sentimental attachment as a phenomenon that begins early in childhood and discusses how particular objects can acquire special significance.Similarly, a 2022 study in Early Child Development and Care, based on an online survey of 700 parents of children aged zero to nine, found that the ways children interacted with attachment objects changed with age. Younger children tended to use cloths and soft toys through physical contact, while older children were more likely to prefer soft toys and treat them as if they had personalities.The researchers suggested that attachment objects may help reduce stress responses, although the survey design does not establish that the objects alone caused this effect.The findings also point to an important distinction: the meaning of a favourite toy can change as a child grows. For one child, it may primarily offer tactile comfort; for another, it may become part of imaginative play, storytelling or pretend conversations.When should parents be concerned?In most cases, a child who wants to carry the same toy around the house does not need to be discouraged. Nor should parents assume that the habit signals anxiety, insecurity or a problem with attachment.The more useful question is whether the object supports the child's everyday life or consistently prevents the child from participating in it.If a toddler carries a soft toy while moving between rooms, plays happily with it nearby and occasionally leaves it behind without distress, there is generally little reason to intervene. The object can be allowed to remain part of the child's routine.Parents can also use the toy to help make transitions easier. For instance, a child starting preschool may be allowed to take an appropriate comfort object if the school permits it. During a change in routine, caregivers can acknowledge the child's feelings rather than insisting that the child should be too old to need the toy.At the same time, parents can gently encourage other ways of coping. They might offer a cuddle, explain what will happen next, maintain predictable routines or help the child name feelings such as fear, sadness and frustration. The aim is not to remove a source of comfort abruptly, but to gradually broaden the child's range of coping strategies.If separation from the object repeatedly triggers extreme distress, or the child's distress substantially interferes with sleep, preschool attendance, play or everyday activities, parents can discuss the pattern with a paediatrician or child-development professional. Such concerns need to be considered in context rather than inferred from the attachment alone.Practical safety matters, too. Small parts, loose buttons, damaged stuffing and long cords can pose risks, while toys taken outdoors may need regular cleaning. Parents should also follow age-appropriate safe-sleep guidance and avoid placing soft objects in an infant's sleep space.The takeaway for parentsA child who carries the same toy from room to room may simply enjoy playing with it. But when the object is consistently sought during transitions, tiredness or distress, it may also be serving as a source of emotional reassurance.The research on attachment objects suggests that familiar possessions can help some children cope with separation and unfamiliar experiences. It does not mean that every child who carries a toy is anxious, or that children who do not have a favourite object are missing an important developmental experience.For parents, the best response is to observe the pattern without rushing to interpret it. Sometimes, the worn teddy bear or much-loved soft toy is not getting in the way of independence. It is helping a child feel secure enough to explore the world beyond it.You use AI every day. articles.title: Rahul Gandhi acquitted in 2018 defamation case over remarks on Amit Shah
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: A special MP/MLA court in Sultanpur on Monday dismissed a 2018 criminal defamation case against Lok Sabha leader of opposition and Congress MP
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A special MP/MLA court in Sultanpur on Monday dismissed a 2018 criminal defamation case against Lok Sabha leader of opposition and Congress MP Rahul Gandhi regarding his remarks against Amit Shah.The case against Rahul relates to alleged objectionable remarks he made about Amit Shah, who was then the BJP president, at a rally in Bengaluru ahead of the 2018 Karnataka assembly elections."This matter dates back to May 2018, when, during a press conference in Bengaluru, Rahul Gandhi made objectionable remarks about the then-national president of the BJP, Amit Shah," said Kashi Prasad Shukla, one of the counsel in the case, as quoted by news agency ANI."He referred to him as an accused in a murder case," he added.Vijay Mishra, a local BJP politician and former chairman of the District Cooperative Bank in Sultanpur, filed a defamation complaint against Gandhi on August 4, 2018. The Congress leader appeared before the court in 2023 and secured bail.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: In 2022, an Indian woman moved to Ireland to study at Trinity College Dublin; four years later, now 25, she is using her real deportation notice in a comedy act after visa delays cost her a job
articles.summary: An Indian woman who moved to Ireland for higher studies in 2022 is now reading her own deportation notice during stand-up comedy performances in Dublin.
articles.body: An Indian woman who moved to Ireland for higher studies in 2022 is now reading her own deportation notice during stand-up comedy performances in Dublin. Jaishree Malik, 25, from Gurugram, had completed her studies at Trinity College Dublin and was working at the university when problems with her immigration permission disrupted her career. After months of waiting for an extension and losing her job, she received a government letter proposing her deportation. She now plans to return to India voluntarily on November 14.Jaishree's deportation letter arrived on October 5, following a lengthy dispute over her right to remain and work in Ireland. She has since made the document part of her performances at comedy clubs. According to The Guardian, at one show, she opened an envelope and began reading the official notice, leaving some audience members unsure whether they were hearing a joke or witnessing something real.The document stated that the Irish authorities were considering a deportation order under the Immigration Act 1999. Jaishree then asked the audience, “Did you know you were friends with a criminal?” “I’m sorry you had to find out this way,” she added.For Jaishree, the performances have become a way to discuss an experience that has affected her employment, finances and plans for the future. She has received job offers during her attempts to resolve her immigration status but has been unable to take them up. Although she is facing a proposed deportation order, she has decided to leave Ireland herself rather than wait for further action.How a visa extension affected her careerJaishree came to Ireland to pursue a Master of Philosophy in literature at Trinity College Dublin. She also worked at the university while studying, helping students with international exchange and study-abroad programmes.After completing her degree, she received permission to remain in the country for two years under the Third Level Graduate Scheme. The arrangement allows eligible international graduates time to find employment and pursue the permission required to continue working.Jaishree remained employed at Trinity and later moved into a role organising events at its law school. However, she needed an extension of her immigration permission to continue working and pursue a longer-term work permit.According to a May report by the Dublin Inquirer, she applied for additional time approximately two months before her Irish Residence Permit expired. By the time the publication interviewed her, she had been waiting around eight months for a decision.The delay meant she could not continue working. She lost her job in February 2026 after being informed that she did not have permission to work while the application was being processed.She had also found an employer willing to support a work permit application. But obtaining that permit depended on having valid immigration documentation.The Guardian later reported that Jaishree received an offer from a government department that she could not accept because her immigration position remained unresolved. “It’s so absurd. I’m being offered a job by the government that I can’t take because of the government,” she said.Immigration troubles became comedy materialLosing her job did not mean Jaishree could stop paying her expenses. She continued living in Dublin using her savings while managing rent and repayments on a student loan taken in India.As the months passed without a resolution, she began spending more time at open mic comedy events. She had previously tried comedy at Trinity College, but had little experience performing at venues around Dublin.Initially, she found it difficult to deliver jokes confidently. She read material from her phone and struggled to judge when to pause. Encouragement from other comedians helped her continue.Her immigration problems gradually became the subject of her performances. In May, the Dublin Inquirer reported that she was already joking about the long wait for a decision on her application.By October, the material had changed again. The government letter gave her something she could physically bring on stage, allowing audiences to hear the language used in the official notice.Some people assumed the routine was fictional. Jaishree said they were surprised when she explained that the events she described had actually happened.Immigration delays have become a concernOther international graduates in Ireland have also reported difficulties obtaining permission to continue working in the country. In May, the Dublin Inquirer reported that Ireland's Department of Justice had approximately 2,700 applications involving extensions of student immigration conditions awaiting processing.The department said the time taken to process applications could depend on several factors, including the number of requests, their complexity and whether additional information was needed.It also explained that the relevant extension process was intended for unforeseen or unusual circumstances, rather than simply providing graduates with additional time to secure a work permit.Immigration solicitor Imran Khurshid told the Dublin Inquirer that such extensions had previously been granted more readily in some cases, but applicants were now experiencing longer waits.But Jaishree has decided to leaveAfter receiving the October 5 notice, Jaishree decided to return to India voluntarily. She is not being forcibly deported, and her departure is scheduled for November 14. Until then, she plans to continue performing comedy in Dublin.Despite her frustration with the immigration process, Jaishree said her experience of living in Ireland has also included strong friendships and support from audiences.“I’m talking about visas, yes, but under this I am still a person. I’ve made a lot of Irish friends who are basically family, and they’re all outraged on my behalf.”Jaishree has also spoken about the prospect of adjusting to life in India after several years abroad. “I don’t think it’ll hit me until I’m on the plane,” she told The Guardian.You use AI every day. articles.title: AO recycles record number of fridges over summer
articles.summary: A peak in production stretched to six weeks, with up to 580,000 appliances passing through the site.
articles.body:
A recycling plant in Telford says it handled a record number of fridges over the summer as the hot weather caused more appliances to break down.

Retailer AO, which operates the Halesfield plant, said June and August were its busiest months ever for fridge recycling.

Summer 2026 was the UK's hottest on record, according to the Met Office, leading to more white goods failing and needing to be scrapped.

Dave Ware, commercial director at AO, said the company was potentially having its biggest year, with between 570,000 and 580,000 fridges coming through its doors.

"What we had was... the hottest temperatures ever, and high temperatures kill fridges in a household," he said.

Ware said the length of this summer's heatwaves had made it particularly challenging, as it meant a longer peak in the number of units being recycled.

"The volume of fridges being recycled across the country was significantly higher than we've ever seen, and for a much longer period of time. The peak is usually seven to 10 days; we're talking five to six weeks," he said.

In August, dozens of councils were forced to stop collecting white goods because of a major backlog, caused by a national shortage of the specialist facilities needed to safely process the appliances.

The backlog was made worse by the closure of three of the UK's 10 full-scale processing plants in the past 14 months, while the remaining sites cannot operate in temperatures above 30C.

Ware said keeping the plant's 80-tonne crushing machine, Bertha, cool was important in order to safely remove pollutants from the appliances.

"We've got some investments coming in terms of cooling the plant more, so we don't have that downtime, and we've also invested in a little bit more storage space as a buffer if there was a problem," he said.

He added that the company had already started planning for a possible surge in fridges and freezers needing recycling next summer if it was as hot as 2026.

"We haven't started taking bets in the office yet on what that's going to be... but I'm learning about El Niño and the effects of that," Ware said.

"It's trying to predict the unpredictable, which is the British summer."
