articles.title: Dragos founder Rob Lee helped bring free cybersecurity to more than 100 utilities; now his company is joining Accenture and SANS on a $10 million plan to protect up to 500 more US water, power and gas providers
articles.summary: Accenture, the industrial cybersecurity firm Dragos and the SANS Institute have launched the Community Cyber Resilience Foundation.
articles.body: Accenture, the industrial cybersecurity firm Dragos and the SANS Institute have launched the Community Cyber Resilience Foundation. It is a non-profit organisation which will offer small and under-resourced US water, electric and natural gas utilities free help securing their operational technology. In its first phase, the foundation will offer cybersecurity software, hardware, deployment services and SANS training at no cost to up to 500 utilities. The three founders are making an initial combined commitment of about $10 million in funding and services, and the data company Elastic is also supporting the effort.New foundation aims to protect critical infrastructureThe three organisations announced the creation of the Community Cyber Resilience Foundation, a nonprofit initiative designed to provide operational technology (OT) cybersecurity tools, deployment services, hardware support and training at no cost to eligible utilities. The programme targets smaller and under-resourced providers that often lack the funding and workforce needed to defend against increasingly sophisticated cyber threats.According to the announcement, the first phase of the initiative will support up to 500 utilities serving communities across the United States. The partners said the combined investment of roughly $10 million will help strengthen services relied upon by more than 100 million Americans.Building on Dragos’ free programmeThe foundation builds on the Dragos Community Defense Program, which already gives more than 100 utilities free access to the Dragos Platform. Dragos was founded by Robert M. Lee, who is its chairman and CEO. Elastic’s role is technical: its Elasticsearch technology provides the main log storage and search engine inside the Dragos Platform, which helps Dragos deliver the software at scale. The foundation was announced at a roundtable on utility cybersecurity in Ohio hosted by Ohio Power Company, an American Electric Power subsidiary, together with Accenture and Dragos.Rob Lee warns of growing threatsAnnouncing the programme, Robert M. Lee said threat actors are increasingly targeting the operational environments that provide essential services to millions of Americans."Adversaries are aggressively targeting utilities, attacking the operational environments that provide life-sustaining services to millions of Americans. Yet many small operators lack the capacity to defend against these threats," Lee said. "The Community Cyber Resilience Foundation gives the utilities that need it most access to cybersecurity resources and training at no cost."What utilities will receiveEligible US-based water, wastewater, electric and natural gas utilities with less than $100 million in annual revenue will be able to apply for the programme. Participants will receive access to the Dragos Platform, deployment and integration support from Accenture, specialised ICS and OT cybersecurity training from SANS, funding for required hardware and infrastructure, and access to a community network of peer utilities.The initiative is also being supported by Elastic, whose technology will help deliver the Dragos Platform at scale to participating organisations.What the executives saidJulie Sweet, Accenture’s chair and CEO, said the work has revealed a widening gap between large operators with the means to invest in cybersecurity and smaller utilities that often lack it. Lee said adversaries are aggressively targeting the operational environments that provide life-sustaining services and that many small operators cannot defend against them alone. James Lyne, SANS’ CEO, said even the best security technology will not protect a utility if its staff cannot use it, which is why the foundation focuses on training. Elastic CEO Ashutosh Kulkarni said his company is committed to helping make advanced capabilities accessible to utilities that could not otherwise afford them.You use AI every day. articles.title: Couple were celebrating anniversary before Bahamas tragedy
articles.summary: Leanne Gregory, from Stapleford in Nottinghamshire, died trying to save her sons swept out to sea.
articles.body:
The husband of a woman who died as she tried to rescue her two sons when they were swept out to sea in the Bahamas said they had been celebrating their 10th wedding anniversary.

Leanne Gregory, from Stapleford in Nottinghamshire, had been on a family holiday with husband Nathan when he believes their boys were swept into the ocean by a riptide.

Although the children were rescued from the water on Tuesday, their mother was unable to be saved, the Royal Bahamas Police Force said.

Speaking to the BBC on Sunday, Nathan, who is now back home with their sons, said the trip had been an early celebration for their anniversary in December.

He said both boys had been so excited and been snorkelling in shallow water as they sorted out their towels and bags on the beach when the boys got into difficulties.

Both parents went into the sea and tried to save them as they were swept out by the current, he added, and the whole ordeal happened in less than 10 minutes.

Nathan said the loss of his 36-year-old "childhood sweetheart" was "unimaginable", but she was a "hero... in life and in death" as she helped to rescue the two boys.

"I've known her since infant school," he told the BBC. "We first got together when we were 14... so 22 years."

"There are no words I can use to describe Leanne, same as anyone she has ever known.

"She was the purest of people, the most generous kind and beautiful person who ever walked the Earth.

"Our relationship was perfect. She was the perfect mother, the perfect wife, the foundation of our entire family."

Nathan added: "Royal Caribbean and Virgin Airlines were absolutely incredible to us and made an impossible journey home so much easier."

Now, as he "keeps strong for his boys", a fundraising page has generated nearly £9,000 in donations to support the family.

More tributes have been paid to the family since the tragedy.

Councillor Richard MacRae, who represents Stapleford north on Broxtowe Borough Council, said it was a "tight-knit community" that would rally around the family.

"It's sad, it's heartbreaking, when something tragic happens and people have got young kids involved, it is just a different level," he said.

"My thoughts and prayers are with the family and friends and the wider community."

On a BBC Facebook post, people passed on their condolences.

One post read: "Grateful to have known you and worked with you Leanne!

Stapleford Fire Station posted it was "deeply saddened" to hear of the mother of two's death.

They said: "Our thoughts are with her family and friends at this difficult time."

The two children were rescued off the coast of Bimini, police in the Bahamas said.

In a statement posted on social media, the Royal Bahamas Police Force said officers received reports shortly after 10:00 local time on Tuesday that a woman had been found unresponsive at the North Bimini Ferry Dock.

It added after she was swept away, she was brought to the ferry dock where CPR was given.

Leanne was then taken to a local medical clinic but was confirmed dead there, the police force said.

It said an autopsy would be conducted but "foul play is not suspected".

A spokesperson for the Foreign Office added: "Our thoughts are with the family of a British woman who has died in the Bahamas.

"We are in contact with the local authorities and providing support to her family."

articles.title: 'Insult to India itself': Rajnath Singh attacks Kharge over 'baap' remark against PM Modi
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Defence minister Rajnath Singh on Monday criticised Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge over his “baap” remark about Prime Minister Narendra
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Defence minister Rajnath Singh on Monday criticised Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge over his “baap” remark about Prime Minister Narendra Modi, saying the comments were an insult to India and an attack on the dignity of politics."I believe this is not merely an insult to an individual or a family, but to India itself. This is also an assault on the dignity of politics. In a democracy, you may register your opposition, question policies, and criticize the government—but please, do not cross the boundaries of personal decorum," he said.He also said that PM Modi could not be swayed by such remarks and that his resolve to serve the people would not be weakened.He said the public kept track of political conduct and would give a fitting response when the time came."The Congress should remember that in a democracy, the public keeps track of everything and, when the time comes, provides a fitting response. I wish to make it clear to the Congress that Prime Minister Modi cannot be swayed by such remarks, nor can his resolve to serve the people be weakened in any way," he said.He further accused Congress of justifying the remarks saying, "But the Congress did not stop there; they are now further hurting people's sentiments by attempting to justify Kharge ji’s words. Instead of acknowledging their mistake and expressing regret, the Congress is busy defending and validating this statement..."The BJP’s Patna Metropolitan unit held a protest march against Kharge’s remarks.The controversy erupted during an event in Patna marking the 139th birth anniversary of Bihar’s first chief minister, Krishna Sinha. When an attendee interrupted Kharge’s address by saying that PM Modi would "not go anywhere", the Congress president reportedly retorted, “Modi ka baap bhi jayega” (Even Modi’s father will have to go).The remark triggered a political row, with the BJP accusing Kharge of using offensive language against the prime minister’s family.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: India’s luxury retail paradox: Too many malls, yet not enough
articles.summary: When Ansal Plaza opened in 1999, it was something Delhi had never seen.
articles.body: When Ansal Plaza opened in 1999, it was something Delhi had never seen. A semi-circular structure with an air-conditioned food court, the city’s first Shoppers Stop and a McDonald’s where getting a table needed luck. For a generation of Delhiites, going there felt like an event. “Visiting Planet M and discovering new music was a thing for us. But now even entering that mall is scary,” says Sheetal Singh, 37, who frequented the mall during her school days.She’s not wrong. Walk through Ansal Plaza today and shuttered fronts outnumber open ones. Corridors echo with footsteps of a handful of people. Instead of the bustle of shoppers, there is the flutter of pigeons.Now drive to DLF Emporio in Vasant Kunj or The Chanakya. The difference is stark. The tenant roster includes Valentino, Jimmy Choo, Louis Vuitton and Dior. Behind the scenes, global luxury houses are waiting for space. But most of them are told the same thing: Aap kataar mein hain.One part of Delhi has malls with empty shops. Another has brands waiting to get into the right ones. The city does not have too many or too few malls. It has a large volume of the ‘wrong’ kind.Delhi is not the only city living this contradiction. Bengaluru has ghost malls, even as destinations such as Mall of Asia and UB City cater to premium shoppers. Mumbai has underperforming malls, alongside luxury destinations such as Jio World Plaza and Phoenix Palladium. Kolkata too has ghost malls, while Quest Mall serves as its luxury retail anchor. These are also cities where international brands are actively looking to expand. Yet the paradox persists: India has an abundance of retail space, but a scarcity of the right kind.‘Top brands are ready to enter India, but there’s no space’India has only three true luxury malls: DLF Emporio and The Chanakya in Delhi, and Jio World Plaza in Mumbai, as per Reuters. Earlier this year, Saurabh Bharara, head of luxury malls at DLF, told Reuters that LVMH, Kering and Richemont regularly ask for more space. “We have top 15 brands that are ready to enter India if we give them space tomorrow,” he said, adding that there was “zero availability”. The shortage is stark. Patek Philippe and Loro Piana have no physical stores in India. Prada has no fashion stores and only one beauty store. Chanel has one fashion store and select beauty boutiques. But, in China and Tokyo, comparable brands operate 14-18+ flagship stores. These markets have luxury retail clusters across multiple locations and neighbourhoods.“There are more brands that want to enter the Indian market but real estate hasn’t caught up,” says Samir Gadhok, co-founder of Burgundy Brand Collective. For some brands, he says, the wait to reach the presentation stage can stretch to 12-18 months. “The supply has not even been close. There is a very real supply wall. There are huge gaps in most tier-1 cities,” says Anuj Kejriwal, CEO of Retail at Anarock Group.Nirzar Jain of Nexus Malls, which operates a portfolio of shopping centres across India, says conversations with prospective tenants often begin well before a store can open. “Some of the conversations actually start a year, year and a half in advance,” he says. With most of the mall portfolio already leased, accommodating a new brand involves mapping lease expiries and identifying suitable space. Brands, meanwhile, need time to study the market and finalise their Indian retail partners.The constraint is not simply the number of stores available. “We would like to accommodate everybody, but that’s not always possible because of constraints of size, availability and sometimes just the market fit,” Jain says.Why old malls are difficult to fixWhy can’t existing malls simply be upgraded? Many were built when organised retail was still finding its feet, and were poorly planned or designed around outdated shopping patterns.Also, ownership fractures the vision. Architect Goonmeet Chauhan points to the strata-selling model, in which individual units are sold to different owners. Coherent curation then becomes difficult. “Ansal Plaza made the mistake of selling,” he notes. Milin Rohinesh, Head of Retail at Cushman & Wakefield India, shares, “When you have individual owners, every decision becomes a negotiation. They all do not have a common vision.”Consumer memory is harder to erase than walls. “If a ghost mall is sitting in a location for five years, the consumer remembers that they haven’t been there for half a decade,” Rohinesh says. A new facade or brighter lighting cannot erase that memory.Sometimes the building itself is the problem. Repositioning requires redesigning the layout, accommodating larger stores, rebuilding the tenant mix, renegotiating leases and upgrading infrastructure. “Mall developers often perceive that building an entirely new asset from the ground up is cheaper and easier,” Kejriwal says.But a vacant mall is not automatically a lost cause. Asked whether an underperforming mall in Delhi could be turned into a luxury destination, Jain says it would depend on the location, catchment and the curation required to make it relevant to customers. “If there was one more mall in Delhi to do, the answer is yes, we would definitely look at it. But evaluate it on its merit and then create the positioning accordingly," he says.This explains the paradox: India has mall space, but not the large, modern, well-located space global brands demand. Ghost malls are often half a million square feet or smaller, says Rohinesh, while newer developments approach or cross a million.An empty shop isn’t available spaceWhy can’t brands simply move into one of the many existing malls? Because the right space is about more than size.“The availability of space does not necessarily make it the right location,” says Sathyajit Radhakrishnan, CEO of Galeries Lafayette India and International Mono Brands at Aditya Birla Fashion and Retail. “Scale, catchment, accessibility and surrounding environment – all have to work together.”A Grade-A or Grade-A+ mall is professionally managed, institutionally owned, designed for large-format stores and curated for the right mix of brands. A Grade B or Grade C mall is older, often strata-owned, and typically lacks the infrastructure, management and tenant mix that premium brands require.A Grade-A mall is increasingly expected to be a destination: shopping, entertainment, dining, hospitality and offices under one roof. Premium brands need larger stores, strong facilities management and the right mix of neighbouring brands. They want spaces that give people a reason to stay, not simply shop. “The arrival experience starts from something as basic as the parking lot,” says Rohinesh.For luxury brands, even visibility has to be carefully considered. “Earlier people believed if their shop was on the main road, it would be successful. But when it comes to premium luxury brands, concealing is important,” says Goonmeet.“What’s more important to them now is who your neighbours are, who your adjacencies are,” explains Gadhok. That is why an empty shop in a struggling mall cannot simply be equated with available space. A brand may have the square footage it needs but still lack the catchment, neighbours, infrastructure or environment it wants.For Jain, the challenge is also one of balancing a growing brand universe with finite space. “We are 98% leased,” he says. “The universe of brands, domestic and international, is growing and there is more demand. Consumption has increased.”That demand is changing what retailers expect from physical stores, too. “Online offers convenience, value and discounted formats, while offline offers experience, better fashion,” Jain says. For higher-priced products such as watches and bags, he adds, customers want to experience the size, colour, quality and detailing in person. The two channels, he argues, coexist rather than replace each other.“It is not constructing a shell, cutting up the shell into multiple small or big stores, adding some escalators, having some glitzy lobby and then having people come there,” Rohinesh says, adding, “Retail space is very scientific.”A mall is no longer the only answerFor brands unwilling to compromise – and unable to wait for new malls – the mall is no longer the only answer.Galeries Lafayette’s India entry is one example. The Parisian department store, brought to India by ABFRL, opened in two restored colonial buildings in Mumbai’s Kala Ghoda rather than a conventional mall. “The choice of Kala Ghoda was deliberate,” says Radhakrishnan. “South Mumbai has the consumer base we are looking to cater to, while Fort offered a setting where fashion, culture and experiences could come together.”The standalone format was not simply a workaround for the shortage of mall space. But for brands that want a conventional mall presence, the shortage remains. Delhi and Mumbai are not the only cities where developers are betting on new formats. Luxury-focused malls are also being planned in eight major cities in the country, including Hyderabad, Ahmedabad, Pune, Kolkata, and Chennai but all are still some years away.Across the market, brands are increasingly pursuing two strategies: find an iconic standalone location, or wait for a Grade-A mall. What they will not do is compromise on size, floor, zoning or neighbours simply to get in. “They will take their time,” says Rohinesh.The Grade-A mall space shortage, in numbersThe shortage of Grade-A malls becomes clearer in the numbers. India has only about 110 million square feet of Grade-A mall stock, compared with more than 400 million in China and around 700 million in the US, according to Anarock. In the first half of 2026, retailers leased 4.1 million square feet of Grade-A mall space across the top seven cities, while developers delivered just 0.9 million square feet of new supply, a demand-to-supply ratio of 4.5 to one. Grade-A mall vacancy has fallen to a 16-year low of 6.7 per cent.Delhi-NCR was the only one of the top seven cities to add Grade-A mall space in H1 2026, with around 0.9 million square feet of new supply, according to Anarock. Bharti Real Estate is developing The Mall at Worldmark at Aerocity, part of a nearly three-million-square-foot retail development, which is expected to add 200,000 square feet of luxury retail to Delhi’s supply.The market is effectively splitting in two: a large stock of ageing malls that shoppers have abandoned, and a small pool of premium destinations that brands are fighting to enter. Retail leasing fell 24 per cent in the first half of 2026, while new completions fell by 57 per cent, according to Anarock. “For supply to catch up, institutional investors must commit to large-scale, experience-led developments in major consumption hubs,” says Kejriwal.But the next generation of retail may not look like the mall of 1999. Goonmeet Singh Chauhan, the architect behind Select City Walk, expects more experiential, family-centric and tourism-oriented destinations, where hotels, offices, wellness centres, cafes and indoor and outdoor experiences sit alongside retail.Jain, too, expects his company to expand beyond its current footprint. Nexus Malls operates in 15 cities and, he says, aims to reach 20-22 cities over the next four to five years, while doubling its portfolio. The expansion, however, will depend on finding the right opportunities, including state capitals and deeper growth in existing markets.The question is no longer whether India has enough mall space. articles.title: Liverpool's bold Virgil van Dijk replacement announces himself
articles.summary: Virgil van Dijk's true successor has fully announced himself now. What a bold signing this would be for Liverpool.Yes, we're firmly at the stage now where Li...
articles.body:
Virgil van Dijk 's true successor has fully announced himself now. What a bold signing this would be for Liverpool.

Yes, we're firmly at the stage now where Liverpool actually have to consider Virgil van Dijk's successor. The Dutchman is turning 36 next summer and his contract will expire.

We're no longer sure that Liverpool will renew it. Van Dijk is defying all historical precedent with his current displays but time will inevitably catch up with him. The club will not want to have their captain on massive deal when he does finally drop out of the elite level.

That may simply mean there's no new contract arriving. But even if it does, Liverpool need to make sure they've got his successor lined up. Maybe that's Jeremy Jacquet but putting all of their eggs in that basket won't be enough.

For one, Liverpool only have Jacquet and Giovanni Leoni contracted to them at centre-back beyond this season. They will need to sign more defenders and that means finding players who can step into Van Dijk's shoes alongside the Frenchman.

There was a lovely reminder in midweek that Jacobo Ramon is truly the next big thing at centre-back. There is arguably no player more primed to take over from Van Dijk as the world's dominant centre-back as the Spaniard.

Ramon is 6ft 5, he's quick, he's still only 21 and he's just completed one of the best seasons in Europe. Our Value Adder model had him as the 6th most valuable centre-back in Europe's top five leagues last season when adjusted for league strength.

He was the only centre-back under 24 in the top 20 and one of only three in the top 35. A special, special talent, in other words.

But it's how he brings this value that draws Van Dijk comparisons. In fact, 2023/24 Van Dijk is one of the two most similar attacking profiles to Ramon last season.

He had considerably more shots than anyone else at centre-back in Serie A last season (over 3 standard deviations above the mean). Ramon sat 2 std above the mean for aerial duels, too, and was above the 93rd percentile among centre-backs for weighted attacking actions and just completing passes in general.

The fact he was also a part of a fantastic defence at Como just adds to it. A brilliant defender with the attacking qualities of Van Dijk and he's only 21.

And then there was that reminder. Ramon helped dominate a game against Manchester United, one in which they took a commanding 4-0 lead before conceding a consolation in stoppage time.

The defender himself capped this off, storming up the pitch to score from open play in a display of elite confidence. This is the player Liverpool need to replace Van Dijk - someone operating on a different level to the rest, much as the Reds' captain has done for years.

articles.title: Canelo Álvarez Arrives in Riyadh; Mexico vs The World Card Proceeds
articles.summary: Fighters are arriving in Saudi Arabia with plans for the October 31 card to take place as scheduled.
articles.body:
Fighters on the "Mexico vs the World" card in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, have begun safely arriving in preparation for the event scheduled on Saturday, October 31

The fight card headlined by Canelo Álvarez vs Christian Mbilli is still scheduled and apparently going forward while violent attacks continue in Saudi Arabia and the Middle East.

Fight Week events begin on Wednesday, October 28, with grand arrivals.

Despite continued security concerns due to political unrest and violence targeting Saudi Arabia, fighters have begun arriving in Riyadh in advance of the "Mexico vs the World" fight card scheduled on Saturday, October 31, with Fight Week activities scheduled to kick off on Wednesday.

WBC World Super Middleweight Christian Mbilli of Quebec will make his first title defense against former undisputed super middleweight champion Saul "Canelo" Álvarez of Mexico. The card, titled "Mexico vs the World," also featured matchups between top Mexican champions and contenders with opponents from around the world.

On Sunday night, DAZN Boxing as well as Turki Alalshikh, chairman of the General Entertainment Authority, posted video of Álvarez arriving in Riyadh alongside former undisputed world heavyweight champion Oleksandr Usyk. Álvarez and several of his stablemates have been training at Usyk's gym located in Valencia, Spain.

Also arriving with Team Canelo was WBO World Featherweight champion Rafael "Divino" Espinoza, also training in Spain. Although he wasn't pictured, WBA World Super Middleweight champion Jaime Munguia of Tijuana likely made the trip as well.

Álvarez has insisted for weeks he would fight in Riyadh without regard to any concerns about safety. On his arrival, Canelo said, "I love to be here in Riyadh, and I'm excited to fight on Saturday, so I can be a world champion again."

Mbilli and his stablemate with Eye of the Tiger Management also on the card, super lightweight Arthur Biyarslanov, arrived several days ago, although they reportedly took an alternative route to the Saudi capital.

Eye of the Tiger president Camille Estephan confirmed he would travel on Monday to support his fighters.

Bout Dropped From Card between Biyarslanov and Delgado

However, Biyarslanov apparently won't be in the ring on Saturday. Biyarslanov was originally scheduled to face Lindolfo Delgado of Mexico for the vacant IBF World Super Lightweight title.

But as of Sunday evening, both Delgado and his trainer, Robert Garcia, were still in the U.S. Garcia has been vocal about the lack of travel planning and information provided to him. Both he and Delgado expressed serious concerns about the conditions involved in making the trip.

While in San Antonio, Texas, working the corner of Albert Gonzalez Saturday night, Garcia spoke with reporter Francisco Salazar about the situation . He acknowledged that his fighter Delgado would still want to show up, "because fighters fight."

But from his perspective as Delgado's trainer, Garcia pointed out that even if he and Delgado left from California for Riyadh on Monday, they would be routed through an airport out of harm's way, then drive for several hours to Riyadh, arriving on Tuesday at the earliest. They would end up with just two days to get acclimated, prepare for the fight, and for Delgado to make weight.

"We're a week away from the fight in Saudi. It's on the other side of the world. They never sent us any flights. They still haven't sent us any flights," said Garcia on Saturday night.

"I've been there multiple times … The first three or four days, you're walking around like a zombie. We're falling asleep in the middle of the day. It's tough. Right now, if we were to leave tomorrow … it's already Monday in Saudi. It takes a day to get there. They're going to take us to another airport. We're going to drive five hours, six hours. We're going to get there Tuesday. They're only going to give me Wednesday and Thursday to make weight? To get used to the time change, It's impossible.

"If we would have had our flights a week ago and said we didn't want to go, that would be different. But we were always ready," said Garcia. He said with Delgado's opponent already in Riyadh for several days, it sets up an unfair situation.

In another schedule change, the Middle East Professional Boxing Commission which officially oversees combat sports in Riyadh, declined to authorize Lorenzo Parra of Venezuela (24-1-1, 18 KOs) as an opponent for WBO World Featherweight champion Rafael "Divino" Espinoza of Guadalajara (28-0, 24 KOs) . WBO President Gustavo Olivieri announced on Friday, October 24, that Ricardo Blandon of Nicaragua (21-6, 14 KOs) will step in as a replacement opponent.

No reason has been given why Parra, the WBO number one contender, was not sanctioned for the fight. Blandon, age 34, is a super featherweight who has never fought outside Central America with no notable opponents save a loss to former champion Rene Alvardo in 2024.

However, he fought at 115 pounds as recently as 2022, and at 5-foot-8, he'll give up only five inches to the 6-foot-1 Espinoza.

Featherweight David Picasso of Mexico and super featherweight Reito Tsusumi of Japan have confirmed their safe arrival in Riyadh for their undercard fights.

Fight Week Schedule for Mexico vs the World

All fighters on the card make their first public appearance as the grand arrivals kick off Fight Week events on Wednesday, October 28.

The fight pre-fight news conference takes place on Thursday, October 29, and will air live on DAZN Boxing at 2 p.m. ET/11 a.m. PT (9 p.m. in Riyadh.

Weigh-ins are scheduled on Friday, October 30, also airing live on DAZN Boxing at 2 p.m. ET/11 a.m. PT.

The U.S. State Department is maintaining its travel advisories for the Middle East, including a Level 3: Reconsider Travel advisory for Saudi Arabia including conflict escalation, flight cancellations, and airspace closures. On Oct. 23, all U.S. non-essential government personnel were ordered to return to the U.S. from the region.

A Level 3 alert is labeled "Reconsider Travel" and covers Saudi Arabia, United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Jordan, Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Isreal, and the West Bank. Details here .

The State Department cites active threats from Iranian drone and missile targeting along with attacks and threats from Houthi rebels in Yemen directed at Saudi territory, infrastructure, and American interests. Falling debris from intercepted projectiles also poses a danger. This is not the highest alert level. Level 4 is "Do Not Travel."

Although the King Khalid Airport in Riyadh is reported open, this does not mean a return to normal schedules. Dozens of international fights are still suspended with multiple airlines no longer flying to Saudi Arabia for now. Flights must secure prior permission from Saudi aviation authorities to land or take off.

The governments of Canada and Mexico also continue to warn citizens to avoid all non-essential travel to the region, including Saudi Arabia.

Nevertheless, the Mexico vs the World card appears to be full steam ahead, even if individual fights drop off the card. This is not unusual in boxing, even when drones are launching missiles near the venue.

Canelo Álvarez of Guadalajara, Mexico (63-3-2, 39 KOs) vs. Christian Mbilli of Montreal, Quebec, Canada (29-0-1. 24 KOs) , for Mbilli's WBC World Super Middleweight title

Jaime Munguia of Tijuana, Mexico (46-2,35 KOs) vs.N ikita Zon of Russia (12-0-1, 10 KOs) for Munguia's WBA World Super Middleweight title

Rafael Espinoza of Mexico (28-0,24 KOs) vs. Ricardo Blandon of Nicaragua (21-6, 14 KOs) for Espinoza's WBO World Super Featherweight title

David Picasso of Colima, Mexico (33-1-1, 18 KOs) vs. Carl Martin of the Philippines (28-0, 21 KOs) for the WBC Silver Featherweight title

Bek Nurmaganbet of Kazakhstan (16-0, 14 KOs) vs. Marcos Vazquez Rodriguez of Tijuana, Mexico (21-3-1, 10 KOs), super middleweights.

Reito Tsutsumi of Japan (5-0, 4 KOs) vs. Raymundo Rojas Garcia of Mexico (16-2, 11 KOs) , featherweights

Bryan Leon of Cuba (12-0, 9 KOs) vs. Hector Aguirre of Mexico (7-0, 3 KOs) , super middleweights

Emiliano Rojo Vazquez of Mexico (21-0, 8 KOs) vs. Flavius Biea of Romania (24-3, 12 KOs) , middleweights.

articles.title: Rahu and Ketu in your birth chart: What their placement is believed to reveal about your life
articles.summary: According to Vedic astrology, the Vimshottari Dasha system divides life into planetary periods.
articles.body: According to Vedic astrology, the Vimshottari Dasha system divides life into planetary periods. The Mahadasha of Rahu spans 18 years, making it the second longest, following Venus. Rahu is a lunar node, a shadow planet and not a tangible celestial body. It constantly moves in retrograde, and the Vedic tradition associates it with desire, illusion, foreign lands, sudden changes and technology. The Ketu Mahadasha lasts for 7 Years and is governed by Ketu. This phase frequently signifies a period of deep reflection, spiritual enlightenment, and an inherent release from material bonds or attachments. Rahu draws you towards worldly ambitions and material experience. Ketu, on the other hand, directs us towards liberation, or mokha, guiding us to cultivate detachment and freedom from earthly ties.Rahu and Ketu: The shadow planetsRahu and Ketu are Chhaya Grahas, or shadow planets, and they lack physical form. They depict the points where Moon’s orbit crosses Earth’s path around the Sun. They are invisible but hold a profound impact according to Vedic astrology. Your thinking, decision-making challenges and overall direction in life are impacted by their placement in your kundli. They have a strong connection to Karmic patterns and show an astrologer why a specific problem keeps repeating in your life. If you know where they are, places in your birth chart can give you real insights of your personality, struggles and natural potential.You can find their origin story in the Puranas when gods won the war and were awarded the nectar of immortality, also called Amrit, during the Samudra Manthan. When a demon named Svarbhanu disguised himself as a god, Amrit, and some of the nectar Lord Vishnu, who was disguised as Mohini, saw through the trick and cut him in two parts with nectar. The head part of Svarbhanu was called Rahu, and the tail was called Ketu.Rahu: The phase of rapid riseThe head part called Rahu is called the snake’s mouth that is never satisfied. It not only craves ‌success and experience but also ‌wealth, authority and fame. It keeps chasing more and more and never feels content in life. It nudges you towards the unknown and big ambitions. It makes you curious and restless and creates longing. This can make a person chase goals at any cost through unconventional ways. If not controlled and understood, it can bring confusion, fear and illusion.Ketu: The phase of letting goThe south node, or the tail, is called the snake’s tail. It does not have a mouth, so it never feels desire or hunger. It is the representation of past learnings like habits, skills and knowledge you carry. Because of Ketu, you may feel detached and lose interest in certain areas of life. It has a peaceful and spiritual influence and pushes you to reflect on life events. A sense of spiritual curiosity prevails and drives you to deeper search. It is linked with mysticism, intuition, solitude and freedom. It helps you to let go of things that are not made for you.What their placement is believed to reveal?Rahu and Ketu sit 180 degrees apart on the birth chart. As they form a karmic axis, Rahu points to where you are meant to grow in this life, and Ketu tells you all the lessons that you got from your past life. As stated by Vedic astrologer Harshit Jain, this axis reveals the balance between your soul’s future growth (Rahu) and your past life mastery (Ketu). Whether your axis falls in the 1–7, 2–8, 3–9, 4–10, 5–11, or 6–12 houses, each placement highlights where you should focus your energy and where you should learn detachment. Understanding this karmic axis can help you make better decisions in relationships, career, finances, spirituality, and personal growth. But other factors also matter along with the Rahu Ketu axis. An astrologer looks at the complete birth chart, planetary aspects, house lords, and dasha for accurate predictions.Rahu Rahu’s mahadasha can bring growth in a career in technology, media, politics, research and aviation. It may open opportunities to travel, work or even settle abroad, and a person may also see a sudden rise in social status. But a person may also face anxiety, struggle with overthinking and feel lost. Risky investments may not be advisable during this time because sudden obstacles may arise.KetuA shift away from worldly desires and towards inner transformation can be felt in the Ketu mahadasha. It can push you towards healing and detachment, where you may feel that you want to let go of pursuits of relationships or material attachments. Since Ketu is linked to past life karmas, during its mahadasha unresolved karmic issues may come up.No dasha plays out in the same way for everyone. articles.title: Edinburgh rejected a 212MW data centre planned with a public park and sports facilities; Scottish Ministers have recalled the appeal amid new scrutiny of large data centres
articles.summary: A proposed green data centre with a public park in Edinburgh has become part of a wider debate over how Scotland should assess large data centre
articles.body: A proposed green data centre with a public park in Edinburgh has become part of a wider debate over how Scotland should assess large data centre developments. The City of Edinburgh Council’s Development Management Sub-Committee voted to refuse the scheme at 1 Redheughs Avenue on 4 February 2026, despite a recommendation from planning officers to grant permission. The decision notice was dated 9 February. Shelborn Drummond Ltd appealed, and Scottish Ministers recalled the appeal on 17 August. The proposal, described in public reporting as a roughly 210MW to 212MW development, includes data centre buildings, supporting infrastructure, sports facilities and active travel routes. The case also involves a dispute over environmental impact assessment, as Scotland introduces new rules for qualifying data centres exceeding 50MW and develops national guidance for hyperscale projects.Why Edinburgh refused the data centre proposalThe application, reference 25/04239/PPP, concerns a proposed green data centre at 1 Redheughs Avenue in the Edinburgh Park and South Gyle area. The council’s planning report describes a scheme comprising data centre buildings, associated infrastructure, landscaping, servicing, car and cycle parking, a public park with sports facilities, and active travel routes. The application sought planning permission in principle, with full approval also sought for specified elements, including the siting of the data centre and public park, maximum building heights, active travel routes and vehicular access points. The Development Management Sub-Committee considered the application on 4 February 2026. Planning officers had recommended approval, subject to conditions and a legal agreement, but the committee voted to refuse permission. The decision notice was dated 9 February.The committee minutes record three principal policy grounds for refusal. Under National Planning Framework 4 (NPF4) Policy 1, the proposal had not demonstrated that it adequately addressed the climate emergency. Under Policy 2, it had not demonstrated that lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions could be minimised. The council also cited City Plan 2030’s Place Policy 19, finding that the proposal did not incorporate a mix of business and residential uses and that its layout did not ensure a cohesive townscape or deliver sustainable movement through the site. The decision differed from the planning officers’ recommendation, which had concluded that the proposal was acceptable overall, subject to developer contributions and other requirements. The disagreement brought the scheme’s energy and climate implications, as well as its fit with the planned character of Edinburgh Park, into focus.The appeal and the environmental assessment disputeShelborn Drummond appealed the refusal to the Scottish Government’s Planning and Environmental Appeals Division (DPEA). The appeal is recorded under reference PPA-230-2794. The DPEA case page lists the appeal as received on 31 March 2026 and records that Scottish Ministers recalled it on 17 August. The case page says the appeal is being considered by ministers. Environmental assessment became a separate issue during the planning process. Edinburgh Council issued two screening opinions, in July and December 2025, concluding that an Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) was not required. A subsequent screening direction by the Scottish Government required an EIA for the proposal, reversing the earlier position that an assessment was unnecessary.Environmental Rights Centre for Scotland, which supported the request for the screening direction, reported that the decision followed representations made on behalf of a client and that the council and developer had opposed the request. The screening direction meant that an EIA report would be required before the appeal could be fully considered. The developer’s agent subsequently indicated that an EIA report would be submitted. The dispute matters because a data centre’s environmental effects can extend beyond the site itself. Scotland’s later national EIA direction identifies issues including energy use, greenhouse gas emissions, water resources, noise, biodiversity and, where backup generators are used, potential air-quality effects. These are matters for environmental assessment, not findings that every impact will necessarily occur at the Edinburgh site.Scotland introduces new rules for data centres above 50MWOn 17 August 2026, the Scottish Government brought a notification direction into force for proposed data centres exceeding 50MW of power capacity. Under the direction, planning authorities must notify Scottish Ministers within seven days of validating a qualifying application and provide the application documents or links to the relevant council webpages. The Chief Planner’s letter explicitly says the requirement applies both to new applications and to applications already being considered. A separate EIA direction was published on 16 September and came into force on 17 September 2026. It requires an EIA for data centre developments exceeding 50MW that fall within the specified industrial-estate or urban-development categories under Scotland’s existing EIA regulations. Developments below the threshold remain subject to case-by-case assessment under those regulations.The Edinburgh proposal has been reported at different power-capacity figures, including around 210MW and 212MW. The exact figure should be taken from the relevant application or technical documents, but the reported estimates are all well above the 50MW threshold. The new national direction is therefore relevant to the wider policy context, although it followed the Edinburgh appeal’s earlier screening dispute and should not be presented as the cause of that decision. The notification and EIA directions serve different purposes. One gives ministers oversight of qualifying applications entering or already within the planning system; the other establishes when an EIA is required for developments within its scope. Together, they reflect the Scottish Government’s decision to require closer scrutiny of large data centre proposals.Parliament calls for national guidance before decisions on hyperscale data centresThe Scottish Parliament debated hyperscale data centres on 16 September 2026 and agreed an amended motion on national planning and spatial guidance. The motion says that new hyperscale data centres should only be approved where they have met robust environmental impact assessments. It also calls for guidance to clarify the conditions under which such developments should be permitted, including consideration of energy use, emissions, water, community benefits and the wider effects on neighbouring communities. The amended motion further states that no planning or consenting decisions on the relevant applications should be made until the guidance has been completed. It calls on the Scottish Government to report to Parliament on progress by the end of 2026 and to publish the guidance in full within 12 months.During the debate, Public Finance Minister Hannah Mary Goodlad said it was “highly unlikely that we will see decisions taken before Christmas”. That was the minister’s stated expectation, rather than a statutory moratorium preventing councils from deciding applications. The parliamentary motion expresses Parliament’s position on the timing of decisions, but does not itself create a legally binding ban. The Government has said it intends to issue updated planning and spatial guidance before the end of 2026. articles.title: A Florida homeowner's house went through foreclosure after he received notice of the trial only after it had finished; on October 23, an appeals court overturned the judgment, ordering a new trial
articles.summary: A Florida homeowner has won an appeal against a foreclosure judgment after he received notice of the trial only after the proceedings had concluded.
articles.body: A Florida homeowner has won an appeal against a foreclosure judgment after he received notice of the trial only after the proceedings had concluded. On October 23, 2026, Florida’s Sixth District Court of Appeal reversed the foreclosure judgment against Robert Dwayne Harris, ruling that the case must return to the lower court for a new trial. According to the court’s opinion available on Justia in Robert Dwayne Harris v. Nationstar Mortgage, LLC, the mortgage company acknowledged that Harris had not received timely notice of the trial, depriving him of an opportunity to present his defences. The ruling restores his opportunity to contest the foreclosure, although it does not itself resolve the underlying dispute.Homeowner challenged the foreclosure judgmentThe case arose from a foreclosure action brought by Nationstar Mortgage, LLC, against Harris in Charlotte County, Florida. Harris appealed the final foreclosure judgment, the denial of his request for a rehearing and the denial of his motion to stop the foreclosure sale. According to the appellate opinion, Harris had been served with the foreclosure complaint and had filed pleadings in response. However, despite participating in the case at that stage, he did not receive notice of the foreclosure trial until after the trial had already taken place.This meant Harris was unable to attend the trial with proper notice and present his arguments against the foreclosure before the judgment was entered. He subsequently brought the notice problem to the attention of the trial court on two occasions, including through a motion for rehearing. The lower court denied that motion without providing a detailed explanation in its order.Harris then challenged the decisions before the Sixth District Court of Appeal, arguing that the foreclosure judgment should not stand when he had not been given a fair opportunity to be heard.Mortgage company acknowledged the notice failureA significant development in the appeal was Nationstar Mortgage’s concession that the judgment had been entered without adequate notice to Harris. The company agreed that the case needed to be sent back for a new foreclosure trial. The appeals court accepted that concession and focused on the procedural defect rather than examining every argument Harris had raised about the underlying foreclosure dispute.The opinion emphasised the importance of notice and the opportunity to be heard in legal proceedings. It cited the principle that a judgment obtained without notice or an opportunity to be heard is void. The court also referred to Florida decisions recognising that notifying people with a legal interest in a case is an essential part of procedural due process. These protections are intended to ensure that parties affected by a court decision have a meaningful opportunity to put forward their claims and defences before a judgment is made. In Harris’s case, the lack of timely notice prevented him from presenting his defences at the foreclosure trial.Appeals court ordered a new trialIn its October 23 decision, the Sixth District Court of Appeal reversed the final foreclosure judgment and remanded the case to the lower court for further proceedings. The court did not decide whether Harris’s substantive defences against foreclosure were valid, leaving those issues for further proceedings in the lower court.The appellate judges also declined to address Harris’s other arguments, including his contention that the trial court had entered judgment without ruling on his motion to dismiss. Because the lack of adequate notice resolved the immediate issue, the court considered it unnecessary to decide the remaining questions at that stage. The ruling therefore gives Harris another opportunity to contest the foreclosure in proceedings where he must receive appropriate notice. It does not amount to a final determination that he is entitled to keep the property or that the mortgage company has no valid foreclosure claim.Foreclosure sale issue remains separateThe appeals court treated Harris’s request to enjoin the foreclosure sale differently from his challenge to the judgment itself. It affirmed the denial of the injunction because the sale had already taken place before the motion was heard, making the request moot. An injunction is generally intended to prevent an anticipated harm, rather than reverse an event that has already occurred. The court cited this principle in explaining why it would not overturn the denial of injunctive relief.However, the opinion noted that reversing the foreclosure judgment could provide grounds for the parties to seek an order from the lower court vacating the foreclosure sale under Florida Rule of Civil Procedure 1.540(b)(5). The reversal does not automatically cancel the completed sale.The appellate decision was therefore mixed: the denial of injunctive relief was affirmed, but the foreclosure judgment was reversed and the case remanded. The next stage will allow the foreclosure dispute to proceed with the required procedural safeguards.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
